items.name: Ada Lovelace
clues: Born in London in 1815. Her famous father left when she was a baby, and she never really knew him.
A mathematician who got very excited about a machine that was never actually built.
In 1843 she published long notes about that machine, including a step-by-step method for it to calculate a series of numbers.
She is often called the first computer programmer.
A programming language is named after her, and a day every October celebrates women in science and technology in her honour.
Her father was the poet Lord Byron. Her title starts with the word “love”.

items.name: Yuri Gagarin
clues: Born in 1934 in a small village west of Moscow. As a teenager he trained to work in a steel foundry, and learnt to fly at a local flying club.
A fighter pilot, chosen in 1960 as one of twenty pilots for a secret training programme.
Just before take-off he said “Poyekhali!”, which means “Let’s go!”. The whole trip took 108 minutes.
On 12 April 1961 he became the first human to travel into space and orbit the Earth.
The UN marks 12 April as the International Day of Human Space Flight. He died in a training flight in 1968, aged 34.
His first name is Yuri, and he flew for the Soviet Union in a capsule called Vostok 1.

items.name: Katherine Johnson
clues: Born in West Virginia in 1918. She was so good at maths that she started high school at the age of ten.
She worked as a “computer”: in those days, that was a job title for a person who did difficult calculations by hand.
In 1962 an astronaut asked for her to check the new electronic computer’s numbers by hand before he flew around the Earth.
One of the Black women mathematicians at NASA whose work was ignored by most history books for decades.
Her story, and the story of two of her colleagues, became the 2016 film Hidden Figures. In 2015 Barack Obama gave her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
Her surname is one of the most common in the USA, and the same as a former British prime minister’s.

items.name: Lewis Hamilton
clues: He grew up in Stevenage, a town north of London, and started racing go-karts at the age of eight.
A sportsman who spends his working life going round in circles, very fast.
At ten he walked up to a team boss at an awards evening and told him he would drive for him one day. A few years later, the team signed him.
The first, and so far the only, Black driver in Formula 1.
Seven world championships, a record he shares with Michael Schumacher. In 2025 he moved to Ferrari.
His first name is the English form of Ludwig, and he is allowed to put “Sir” in front of it.

items.name: Malala Yousafzai
clues: Born in 1997 in the Swat Valley in northern Pakistan, where her father ran a school.
At eleven she wrote an anonymous online diary for the BBC about life in a valley where girls were being banned from going to school.
In 2012, aged 15, she survived an attack on her school bus and was flown to Birmingham for treatment. She stayed in England.
In 2014, at 17, she became the youngest person ever to win a Nobel Prize.
She graduated from Oxford University in 2020, and runs a fund that campaigns for every girl’s right to twelve years of school.
The UN named her birthday, 12 July, after her. She shares her first name with a famous Pashtun folk heroine, Malalai.

items.name: Amelia Earhart
clues: Born in Kansas in 1897. As a girl, she kept a scrapbook of newspaper stories about women doing jobs usually done by men.
She took her first flying lesson in 1921. Her first plane was bright yellow, and she called it “The Canary”.
In 1932 she landed in a field in Northern Ireland, and a surprised farm worker asked her if she had come far.
The first woman to fly alone, without stopping, across the Atlantic.
In 1937 she disappeared over the Pacific while trying to fly around the world. Her plane has never been found.
Her surname sounds like “air heart”, which suits a pilot.
